paragraphs: Children in care in Calderdale are looked after by Calderdale Council's own fostering service and by the independent agencies shown above. The council says the national shortage of foster families is felt in Calderdale too, and it looks for carers for children and young people of every age from birth to 18, for brothers and sisters who need to stay together, and for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children.

The council offers several kinds of fostering. Short-term care can last from a few weeks to a couple of years, while long-term carers look after a child until they are ready to move on to independence. Emergency duty carers take children in a crisis outside office hours, support carers give full-time carers a break for a few days or a couple of weeks, and the short breaks scheme offers disabled children anything from one night a week to one weekend a month.

Calderdale's 2026-27 maintenance allowance follows the government's minimum rates, from £176 a week for a baby to £267 for a young person of 16 or over, and its carers also receive a weekly skill-based payment of between £138.74 and £386.54 depending on their skills and experience; our Calderdale allowance page has the detail. Carers who pay council tax to Calderdale and offer a home for 26 weeks of the year get a full council tax exemption. The council also lists training online and in person, a dedicated fostering social worker, a mentor who already fosters, groups for carers and for their own children, therapeutic support, free Fostering Network membership and its carers' association, Families at Calderdale Together.
Whichever route suits you, speak to the council and to two or three of the services above about the children they most need homes for and the support they give.
